newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Future HK legislators hold extensive business assets.
newsitem.headline: Future HK legislators hold extensive business assets.

text.p: Members of a controversial shadow Hong Kong parliament set up by China have disclosed their business assets for the first time, revealing that 70 percent of the legislators are either shareholders or company directors.
The disclosures were made available for public inspection on Monday across the border in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where the provisional legislature now meets.

Britain is handing back the colony of 6.4 million people at midnight on June 30. China plans to disband the present elected Legislative Council, or Legco, and the provisional legislature will take over until elections are held, possibly a year later.
The new body has made asset disclosure one of its rules.
Reporters who inspected the documents said on Tuesday that 70 percent of the interim body's 60 members owned shares or served on the boards of companies.

Top of the list was Yeung Chun-kam, a textile magnate widely known as the "king of trousers" for his interests in the jeans business. Yeung holds 211 directorships and owns shares in 258 companies, more than twice the number of interests held by the nearest rival on the list, according to the disclosures.
Other members hold business interests in sectors ranging from property and shipping to jewellery, food and kindergartens.
One member, on a trip abroad, failed to register his assets.
Of the 59 who did register, 24 held property abroad.

Leung Chun-ying, whose appointment to head a post-handover taskforce on housing strategy stirred up controversy recently when it was revealed he had properties in Hong Kong, Singapore and China's Shandong province.
The 33 members who also hold seats in Legco seemed confused about what to declare -- half of them forgot to mention their HK$90,000 monthly salaries as Legco members.
Several others forgot to declare allowances they receive as advisers to Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa. Members will have to resubmit their disclosures, filling in the gaps.
